n: A coalition of Moabites, Ammonites, and others (probably Meunites from Edom’s region) came to attack Jehoshaphat.

f.g: The Hebrew is unclear; many read ‘Meunites,’ a people from the region of Seir.

n: Messengers report a huge army coming from across the Dead Sea, already at En-gedi on Judah’s eastern edge — dangerously close.

f.g: Most scholars read ‘from Edom’ (a one-letter difference in Hebrew).
An oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea.

n: Jehoshaphat was afraid — but he responded to fear by seeking the Lord and calling a nationwide fast. Fear rightly handled drives us to God.
People came from every town in Judah to seek the Lord’s help together.
Jehoshaphat stood before the assembly in the temple, in front of the new courtyard, to lead the prayer.

f.g: Perhaps a recently renovated courtyard of the temple.

n: He begins by declaring who God is: the ruler of heaven and all nations, whose power no one can resist. Faithful prayer often starts by remembering God’s greatness.

f.w: art not thou God in heaven?

n: He recalls that God drove out the land’s former inhabitants and gave it forever to the descendants of Abraham, His friend.
Israel lived in the land and built a sanctuary for God’s name.
Jehoshaphat reminds God of Solomon’s dedicatory prayer: when disaster comes and we cry to You before this house, You will hear and save.
These invaders are the very nations God told Israel not to attack during the Exodus, because they were related to Israel through Lot and Esau.

f.w: whom thou wouldest not let Israel invade

n: Now they repay that kindness by trying to drive Israel out of the land God gave them.
One of scripture’s most honest prayers: we have no power against this army and don’t know what to do — but our eyes are on You. Admitting helplessness is itself an act of faith.

f.w: neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee

n: All Judah — men, women, little children — stood before the Lord, waiting for His answer.
The Spirit came upon Jahaziel, a Levite singer descended from Asaph. God answered through an unexpected person in the middle of the congregation.

f.w: came the Spirit of the LORD

n: God’s message: don’t be afraid or discouraged by this great army, for the battle is not yours, but God’s.

f.w: the battle is not yours, but God's

n: God gives specific directions: tomorrow go down to meet them as they come up the pass of Ziz at the end of the valley near the wilderness of Jeruel.

f.g: A pass climbing from the Dead Sea toward Tekoa.

n: You won’t need to fight: take your positions, stand firm, and see the Lord’s deliverance. These words echo Moses at the Red Sea.

f.w: stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD

n: The king bowed with his face to the ground, and everyone fell in worship before the Lord — responding to the promise before seeing it fulfilled.
Levites from the Kohathite and Korahite clans stood and praised God at the top of their voices — celebrating victory in advance.

f.g: Descendants of Korah, temple singers credited with several psalms.

n: Early the next morning Jehoshaphat told the people as they set out: believe the Lord and you’ll stand firm; believe His prophets and you’ll succeed.

f.w: Believe in the LORD your God, so shall ye be established
f.g: A Hebrew wordplay: ‘believe’ (ha’aminu) and ‘be established’ (te’amenu) share a root.

n: He put singers in front of the army to praise the beauty of holiness, singing, “Praise the LORD; for his mercy endureth for ever.” Worship led the way into battle.

f.w: for his mercy endureth for ever

n: As soon as they began singing, the Lord set ambushes against the invaders, and they were defeated.

f.g: Ambushes — perhaps caused by confusion among the enemies themselves.

n: Ammon and Moab turned on the people of Seir and destroyed them, and then turned on each other. God used their own confusion to defeat them.

f.w: every one helped to destroy another

n: When Judah reached the watchtower overlooking the desert, they saw only bodies — no one had escaped.

f.w: the watch tower in the wilderness
f.g: A lookout point overlooking the wilderness.

n: Gathering the spoil — goods, clothing, and valuables — took three full days because there was so much.

f.g: Some manuscripts read ‘garments’ instead of ‘dead bodies.’

n: On the fourth day they gathered in a valley and blessed the Lord, naming it the Valley of Berachah, “Valley of Blessing.”
Everyone returned to Jerusalem joyfully, with Jehoshaphat leading them, because the Lord had given them joy over their enemies.
They entered Jerusalem and went to the temple with lyres, harps, and trumpets — the campaign began and ended in worship.
Nearby kingdoms feared God after hearing how He had fought Israel’s enemies.

f.w: the fear of God was on all the kingdoms

n: Jehoshaphat’s kingdom enjoyed peace, for God gave him rest on every side.
A summary: Jehoshaphat became king at thirty-five and ruled twenty-five years (about 872–848 BC). His mother was Azubah.
He followed in the footsteps of his father Asa and did what was right in God’s sight.
Yet the high places remained, because the people still hadn’t fully set their hearts on God. A king can lead, but each heart must choose.

f.w: the people had not prepared their hearts

n: His full history was written by the prophet Jehu son of Hanani and included in the book of the kings of Israel.
Later Jehoshaphat again allied himself with a wicked northern king — Ahaziah, Ahab’s son. He seems not to have fully learned the earlier lesson.
Together they built a fleet at Ezion-geber to sail to distant ports.

f.g: Large ocean-going ships; 1 Kings 22:48 says they were bound for Ophir.

n: The prophet Eliezer warned that because of this alliance, the Lord would destroy the project. The ships were wrecked before they could sail. Partnerships with the wicked bring loss.
